title: Late Ottoman Anatolia
subtitle: 1800–1908 · The End of the Notables, the Tanzimat, the Hamidian Age and the Railway

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: Mahmud II against the ayans, the men of the Tanzimat, the fall of the Kurdish emirates and Abdülhamid's autocracy

entries.label: Mahmud II and the end of the ayans
entries.hint: Mahmud II, who had seen the notables force a charter on the throne in 1808, broke them one by one: the Çapanoğlu of Yozgat in 1813–1814, the Karaosmanoğlu of Manisa and most of the other houses by the 1830s, and the janissaries in 1826. He built a new army and a centralised bureaucracy. Anatolia was brought back under the capital.
entries.note: Sened-i İttifak (1808); Stanford Shaw, History of the Ottoman Empire and Modern Turkey vol. 2 (1977); Yuzo Nagata, Tarihte ayanlar (1997).

entries.label: The end of the Kurdish emirates
entries.hint: The hereditary Kurdish emirates that had held the frontier since Selim's time, among them Soran, Bohtan, Hakkâri and Baban, were put down by the reforming government between the 1830s and about 1850. The emir Bedirhan Bey of Botan, who had organised a powerful state and had massacred the Assyrian Christians in the mountains, was defeated in 1847 and exiled to Crete. The tribal chiefs and the sheikhs took their place.
entries.note: Martin van Bruinessen, Agha, Shaikh and State (1992); Hakan Özoğlu, Kurdish Notables and the Ottoman State (2004).

entries.label: Reşid, Âli and Fuad Pasha
entries.hint: The statesmen Mustafa Reşid Pasha, Âli Pasha and Fuad Pasha dominated the Tanzimat or 'reordering': the edict of Gülhane, new provincial administrations, new codes and schools. In the provinces their reforms were carried by governors, councils and tax officials, often against local resistance. The empire's government was made more regular and more intrusive.
entries.note: Roderic Davison, Reform in the Ottoman Empire 1856–1876 (1963); Shaw 1977.

entries.label: Ahmed Cevdet and the Fırka-i Islahiye
entries.hint: Ahmed Cevdet Pasha, a historian and jurist, was sent in 1865 with a reform division, the Fırka-i Islahiye, to subdue the nomadic and rebel chiefs of the Cilician mountains, among them Kozanoğlu, and to settle the tribes on the plains. He moved thousands of families to farms, and the Çukurova became a land of cotton and settled villages.
entries.note: Ahmed Cevdet Pasha, Maʿruzat (1980); Cevdet, Tezâkir; Reşat Kasaba, A Moveable Empire (2009).

entries.label: Abdülhamid II
entries.hint: Abdülhamid II came to the throne in 1876, promulgated a constitution, and in 1878 suspended parliament and ruled for thirty years as an autocrat through a network of spies, telegraph lines, schools and pan-Islamic appeals. He founded the Hamidiye cavalry in 1891 from Kurdish tribes. The state grew more centralised, and more repressive.
entries.note: Selim Deringil, The Well-Protected Domains (1998); Shaw 1977; François Georgeon, Abdülhamid II (2003).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: Ibrahim Pasha in Anatolia, the Russian war and the loss of Kars, Sheikh Ubeydullah and the massacres of 1894–1896

entries.label: Ibrahim Pasha in Anatolia
entries.hint: The army of Ibrahim Pasha, son of Muhammad Ali of Egypt, took Syria and crossed the Taurus, and on 21 December 1832 it destroyed the Ottoman army at Konya and captured the grand vizier. The way to Istanbul was open and Mahmud II called in Russian troops. Ibrahim's army was only halted by the convention of Kütahya in 1833.
entries.note: Shaw 1977; Khaled Fahmy, All the Pasha's Men (1997); Henry Dodwell, The Founder of Modern Egypt (1931).

entries.label: Kars and the war of 1877–1878
entries.hint: In the war of 1877–1878 the Russians invaded eastern Anatolia from the Caucasus, took Ardahan and Kars in 1877, defeated the Ottomans in the field at Aladja and besieged Erzurum. The peace left Russia with Kars, Ardahan and Batum, and with thousands of Muslim refugees to move into the heartland.
entries.note: Treaty of San Stefano and Congress of Berlin (1878); William Allen and Paul Muratoff, Caucasian Battlefields (1953).

entries.label: Sheikh Ubeydullah's rising
entries.hint: Sheikh Ubeydullah of Nehri, a Naqshbandi sheikh and landowner, led Kurdish tribesmen in 1880 across the Persian border and into the plain of Urmia, in a movement of Kurdish national and religious claims, which the Ottoman government at first tolerated. It was put down by the Persians and by Ottoman troops, and Ubeydullah was exiled.
entries.note: Wadie Jwaideh, The Kurdish National Movement (2006); van Bruinessen 1992; Sabri Ateş, The Ottoman-Iranian Borderlands (2013).

entries.label: The Armenian revolutionary movement
entries.hint: The Hunchak party (1887) and the Dashnaktsutiun (1890) organised Armenian villagers for self-defence and, in places, for revolt and acts of terror: the Zeytun rising of 1895–1896 and the seizure of the Ottoman Bank in Istanbul by Dashnak militants in August 1896. Historians differ on how far the massacres of the 1890s answered these movements and how far they were a means of crushing the demand for reform.
entries.note: Louise Nalbandian, The Armenian Revolutionary Movement (1963); Gerard Libaridian, Modern Armenia (2004).

entries.label: The massacres of 1894–1896
entries.hint: Following the resistance of Armenian villagers to tax collectors and Kurdish tribal cavalry at Sasun in 1894, massacres of Armenians took place across the eastern provinces and cities from Trabzon to Urfa, in some places led by officials, soldiers and Muslim crowds, and at Urfa in December 1895 burned some thousands of people in the cathedral. Estimates of the dead run from 100,000 to 300,000 on different counts; the sultan's own responsibility is debated.
entries.note: British consular reports (Blue Books on Turkey, 1895–97); Ottoman archives; Vahakn Dadrian, The History of the Armenian Genocide (1995); Selim Deringil, 'The Armenian question is finally closed' (2009); Jelle Verheij in Kieser and Schaller (eds), Der Völkermord an den Armeniern (2002).

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Gülhane edict, the Land Code, the vilayet law, the constitution of 1876, the Public Debt and the Armenian constitution

entries.label: The Gülhane edict
entries.hint: Mustafa Reşid Pasha read before the sultan, the notables and the foreign ambassadors a charter granting every subject, whatever his religion, security of life, honour and property, an end to tax-farming and a regular system of conscription and taxation. It began the era of the Tanzimat.
entries.note: Hatt-ı Şerif of Gülhane (3 November 1839); Davison 1963.

entries.label: The Land Code of 1858
entries.hint: The Land Code classified land, confirmed the rights of long possession, required registration of titles and gave cultivators inheritable use rights, to enlarge the state's tax base. In practice, the registration of land in the names of notables, tribal leaders and merchants consolidated large estates in many regions. The state's claim to the land was reinforced.
entries.note: Ottoman Land Code (Arazi Kanunnamesi, 1858); Halil İnalcık and Donald Quataert, An Economic and Social History of the Ottoman Empire (1994).

entries.label: The Armenian National Constitution
entries.hint: The Ottoman government approved in 1863 a constitution for the Armenian millet which gave its lay members a national assembly alongside the clergy, and set out the powers of the patriarch, provincial councils and schools. It was one of the most developed in the empire. Its debates became a forum for the complaint of the Anatolian Armenians.
entries.note: Nizamname of the Armenian Nation (1860/1863); Roderic Davison; Vartan Artinian, The Armenian Constitutional System in the Ottoman Empire (1988).

entries.label: The vilayet law
entries.hint: The Provincial Law of 1864, modelled on the French departments, divided the empire into vilayets under a governor with appointed officials and elected councils, subdivided in sanjaks, kazas and villages. The new system replaced the sanjak and eyalet divisions and was applied in Anatolia in the following years. It extended the central government's reach.
entries.note: Vilayet Nizamnamesi (1864); Davison 1963; Shaw 1977.

entries.label: The constitution of 1876
entries.hint: The Kanun-ı Esasi, promulgated by Abdülhamid on 23 December 1876, declared all Ottoman subjects equal and set up an elected chamber alongside an appointed senate. The first parliament met in 1877 with deputies from Anatolia, and in February 1878, with a Russian army near the capital, the sultan prorogued it. The text stayed formally in force.
entries.note: Kanun-ı Esasi (1876); Robert Devereux, The First Ottoman Constitutional Period (1963).

entries.label: The Public Debt and the tobacco Régie
entries.hint: After the state's bankruptcy of 1875, the decree of Muharram in 1881 set up the Ottoman Public Debt Administration, controlled by European creditors, with the right to collect the salt, tobacco, stamp, silk and fish taxes. The tobacco monopoly, the Régie, with its guards, was resented in the tobacco country of the Black Sea and the Aegean.
entries.note: Decree of Muharram (1881); Donald Blaisdell, European Financial Control in the Ottoman Empire (1929); Şevket Pamuk, The Ottoman Empire and European Capitalism (1987).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: The American colleges, the Protestant and Catholic millets and the Hamidian Sunni campaign among the Alevis

entries.label: The Catholic and Protestant millets
entries.hint: In 1831 the government recognised the Armenian Catholics and in 1850 the Armenian Protestants as separate millets, with their own leaders and courts. The step reflected the growth of missions and the pressure of the European powers, and divided Armenian communities in Anatolia along new lines.
entries.note: Imperial berats of 1831 and 1850; Davison 1963; Kemal Karpat, The Politicization of Islam (2001).

entries.label: The American colleges in Anatolia
entries.hint: American Protestant missionaries of the ABCFM, who began work among Armenians, Greeks and Syrians in the 1820s and 1830s, founded schools, hospitals and colleges: Robert College in Istanbul (1863), Anatolia College at Merzifon, Euphrates College at Harput and the girls' colleges. They educated much of the Christian middle class and brought western books.
entries.note: ABCFM Annual Reports; Frank Andrews Stone, Academies for Anatolia (1984); Ussama Makdisi, Artillery of Heaven (2008).

entries.label: The Hamidian campaign among the Alevis
entries.hint: Abdülhamid's government, concerned at foreign missionaries and the Kızılbaş and Alevi minorities, sent preachers, built mosques and Sunni schools in Alevi villages, and sometimes obliged them to pay for them. Alevis petitioned and resisted, and the policy of assimilation by schooling and mosque-building was a failure.
entries.note: Selim Deringil, 'The Struggle against Shiism in Hamidian Iraq' (1990); Selim Deringil 1998; Markus Dressler, Writing Religion (2013).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The houses of Safranbolu, the sultan's albums, Dadaloğlu and Komitas

entries.label: The houses of Safranbolu
entries.hint: The merchant town of Safranbolu in the Black Sea mountains has hundreds of timber-framed houses of the 18th and 19th centuries, with overhanging upper floors, wide eaves and carved ceilings. The konaks of other Anatolian towns, such as Amasya, Tokat and Beypazarı, share the style. UNESCO listed Safranbolu in 1994.
entries.note: UNESCO World Heritage List no. 614; Doğan Kuban, Turkish Vernacular Architecture.

entries.label: Dadaloğlu
entries.hint: Dadaloğlu, an Afshar âşık of the Taurus, sang of the horsemen of his tribe and of their grief when the government's division forced them off the mountains in the 1860s, in words that are famous in Turkish: 'if the edict is the sultan's, the mountains are ours'. He is the poet of the last years of the nomads.
entries.note: Dadaloğlu, Şiirleri; Sadettin Nüzhet Ergun, Türk Halk Şairleri.

entries.label: Komitas and the folk song
entries.hint: Komitas (Soghomon Soghomonian), born at Kütahya in 1869 to an Armenian family and orphaned young, became a priest and a student in Berlin, and collected thousands of Armenian, Kurdish and Turkish peasant songs and church chants, which he transcribed, harmonised and performed. He is the founder of modern Armenian music and of Armenian ethnomusicology.
entries.note: Komitas, Armenian Folk Songs (1904–1912); Rita Soulahian Kuyumjian, Archaeology of Madness (2001).

entries.label: The sultan's photograph albums
entries.hint: Abdülhamid II had albums of photographs made of the provinces and their schools, barracks, ships, factories and bridges and gave about fifty to the Library of Congress and the British Museum. They present the Ottoman state as a modern power, with its provincial cities of Anatolia as showpieces.
entries.note: Abdülhamid II albums (Library of Congress, Prints and Photographs Division; British Library); Carney Gavin, Imperial Self-Portrait (1988).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The Mecelle, the Young Ottomans and the rediscovery of ancient Anatolia

entries.label: The rediscovery of ancient Anatolia
entries.hint: European scholars rediscovered ancient Anatolia in the nineteenth century: Charles Texier found Boğazköy in 1834, Schliemann dug at Troy from 1870, John Turtle Wood at Ephesus in the 1860s and Carl Humann at Pergamon in 1878. Osman Hamdi Bey, director of the Imperial Museum from 1881, secured the 1884 antiquities law which kept finds in the empire.
entries.note: Charles Texier, Description de l'Asie Mineure (1839–49); Zainab Bahrani, Zeynep Çelik and Edhem Eldem (eds), Scramble for the Past (2011).

entries.label: The Young Ottomans
entries.hint: A group of writers and officials, among them Namık Kemal, Ziya Pasha and Ali Suavi, argued in the new press that the Tanzimat had given the people neither liberty nor a share in power and that constitutional government was consistent with Islam. They went into exile in Paris and London. They were the first organised constitutional opposition in the empire.
entries.note: Namık Kemal, Vatan yahut Silistre (1873); Şerif Mardin, The Genesis of Young Ottoman Thought (1962).

entries.label: The Mecelle
entries.hint: A commission led by Ahmed Cevdet Pasha compiled the Mecelle-i Ahkâm-ı Adliye, a civil code in 1,851 articles based on Hanafi law and in a modern form, issued in 1869–1876. It was the first codification of Islamic law, in force in the courts of Anatolia and later the Arab provinces until the 1920s.
entries.note: Mecelle-i Ahkâm-ı Adliye (1876); Ahmed Cevdet, Tezâkir; Niyazi Berkes, The Development of Secularism in Turkey (1964).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The Aydın and Anatolian railways, cotton and tobacco, carpet exports and the famine of 1873–1875

entries.label: The Aydın and Anatolian railways
entries.hint: A British company opened the Izmir–Aydın line in 1866, the first Anatolian railway, which carried the fig, cotton and olive oil of the Maeander valley to the port. The Anatolian Railway Company, a German enterprise under Deutsche Bank, built from the Bosphorus to Eskişehir and Ankara in 1892 and Konya in 1896. Lines changed the economy of the districts they served.
entries.note: Orhan Kurmuş, Emperyalizmin Türkiye'ye girişi (1974); Murat Özyüksel, The Berlin-Baghdad Railway (2014); Pamuk 2000.

entries.label: Cotton and tobacco
entries.hint: The American Civil War cut the supply of cotton to Europe and caused a boom in the Çukurova and the Aegean plains in the 1860s, when large lands were planted. Tobacco was grown for export in the Black Sea and Aegean uplands and was largely under the Régie. Cash crops linked Anatolia to world markets.
entries.note: Donald Quataert, Ottoman Manufacturing in the Age of the Industrial Revolution (1993); Pamuk 2000.

entries.label: The famine of 1873–1875
entries.hint: A drought and the failure of the harvests of 1873, with a hard winter and a cattle plague, brought famine to Ankara, Sivas and Kayseri, with a death toll variously estimated in the tens to hundreds of thousands, and an exodus from the worst districts. Relief was inadequate, and the famine contributed to the state's bankruptcy.
entries.note: Quataert 1993; Pamuk 2000; Consular reports; Caroline Finkel, Osman's Dream (2005).

entries.label: The carpet export boom
entries.hint: European demand for oriental carpets in the late nineteenth century brought a boom in weaving, with tens of thousands of village women and girls working to order for European and American firms, often under advances from merchants and with the use of chemical dyes. By 1908 much of the trade was in the hands of a few large foreign firms.
entries.note: Donald Quataert 1993; Consular reports; Oriental Carpet Manufacturers Ltd (1908).

entries.label: The telegraph and the steamer
entries.hint: The first Ottoman telegraph lines were laid in the Crimean War of 1855 and extended across Anatolia in the following decades to every provincial capital, giving the sultan's government the means to receive reports and give orders in hours. Steamships plied the Black Sea and Aegean coasts. Communications changed government.
entries.note: Yakup Bektaş, 'The Sultan's Messenger' (2000); Deringil 1998; Quataert 1993.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The muhacir, German capital and the Armenian emigration

entries.label: The Anglo-Ottoman free trade convention
entries.hint: In 1838 Britain and the Ottoman Empire signed at Balta Limanı a commercial convention that abolished monopolies and internal customs, and limited import duties to 3 per cent. Other European states soon had the same terms. The treaty opened the Anatolian market to British cotton goods, and the weavers of the interior suffered from the competition, though historians now stress that the effects varied by region and product.
entries.note: Convention of Balta Limanı (1838); Quataert 1993; Pamuk 2000.

entries.label: The muhacir
entries.hint: Wars and annexations in the Caucasus, the Crimea and the Balkans drove well over a million Muslims, Circassians, Abkhaz, Crimean Tatars and Balkan Turks, into Ottoman lands in the later nineteenth century, many of them, after the Circassian exodus of 1864, to Anatolia. They were settled in the interior, on land taken from nomads, and in the cities. The refugees changed the character of the country.
entries.note: Kemal Karpat, Ottoman Population 1830–1914 (1985); Justin McCarthy, Death and Exile (1995).

entries.label: German capital and the Anatolian Railway
entries.hint: Deutsche Bank and the Anatolian Railway Company took over the line to Ankara in 1888, built it to Konya by 1896 and in 1903 received the concession for the Baghdad Railway, with the Kaiser's support. German engineers, banks and diplomats were strongly present in Anatolia from then on.
entries.note: Baghdad Railway concession (1903); Edward Mead Earle, Turkey, the Great Powers and the Bagdad Railway (1923); Özyüksel 2014.

entries.label: The Armenian emigration
entries.loc: Eastern Anatolia and the United States
entries.hint: After the massacres of the 1890s and with the help of missionary and relief networks, tens of thousands of Armenians left the eastern provinces for the Caucasus, the United States, France and Egypt. Communities in Worcester, Fresno and elsewhere traced their origins to the villages of Harput, Van and Sivas.
entries.note: Kemal Karpat 1985; Robert Mirak, Torn between Two Lands (1983).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Article 61 of Berlin, the censuses and the new demography

entries.label: The eastern question in Anatolia
entries.hint: Anatolia became the stage of the 'Eastern Question', with Russia pressing from the Caucasus, Britain concerned for the road to India, France and Germany seeking spheres, and the powers claiming protection of Christians. Ottoman efforts to control the provinces were seen through this foreign scrutiny.
entries.note: M. S. Anderson, The Eastern Question (1966); Deringil 1998.

entries.label: Article 61 of the Treaty of Berlin
entries.hint: At the Congress of Berlin in 1878 the Ottomans promised, in Article 61, to carry out reforms in the Armenian provinces and to guarantee the security of Armenians against Kurds and Circassians, under the watch of the powers. The article, never implemented, made the 'Armenian question' an international one.
entries.note: Treaty of Berlin (1878), art. 61; Davison; Hovannisian (ed.), The Armenian People from Ancient to Modern Times vol. 2 (1997).

entries.label: The census of 1881–1893
entries.hint: The Ottoman censuses of 1881–82 and 1893 counted Anatolia's population as roughly three-quarters or more Muslim, with Greeks and Armenians the largest Christian communities, concentrated on the west coast, in the Pontus and in the eastern provinces. The figures, which undercount women and some groups and are contested by every side, are the base of all discussion of the demography of late Ottoman Anatolia.
entries.note: Kemal Karpat, Ottoman Population 1830–1914 (1985); Stanford Shaw, 'The Ottoman Census System and Population, 1831–1914' (1978); Justin McCarthy, The Population of the Ottoman Empire and Turkey (1983).

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The first schools for girls, the carpet weavers, Grace Kimball at Van and the end of the Circassian slave trade

entries.label: The Circassian slave trade and its abolition
entries.hint: The trade in Circassian and Georgian girls and boys through Trabzon, Samsun and Istanbul, which supplied households and the harem, ran alongside the trade in enslaved Africans. A firman of 1857 banned the African trade under British pressure, but both trades continued in practice; the Circassian trade was swollen by the exodus of 1864 and declined only after the 1870s. Slavery itself was never abolished by law in the empire.
entries.note: Ehud Toledano, The Ottoman Slave Trade and Its Suppression (1982); Madeline Zilfi, Women and Slavery in the Late Ottoman Empire (2010).

entries.label: The first schools for girls
entries.hint: The first state school for girls, the Kız Rüşdiyesi, opened in 1859, and in 1870 a training college for women teachers, the Darülmuallimat. Girls' schools spread to Anatolian cities in the following decades, and the missionary schools had their own. Literacy among women was still very low in 1908.
entries.note: Selçuk Akşin Somel, The Modernization of Public Education in the Ottoman Empire (2001); Davison 1963.

entries.label: The carpet weavers
entries.hint: Consular reports describe girls of six or seven years old working long days at looms in the workshops of Uşak and Isparta, with merchants' advances, bad light and ill health. The industry which brought a flow of cash into villages depended on the labour of girls and women who left no records of their own.
entries.note: British consular reports (Smyrna, 1890s–1900s); Quataert 1993.

entries.label: Grace Kimball at Van
entries.hint: Grace Kimball, an American doctor of the missionary board, went to Van in 1897 and ran a hospital for Armenians, Kurds and Turks, a school and a relief programme for survivors of the massacres. She was one of a number of women missionaries who worked in Anatolia as doctors, teachers and administrators.
entries.note: ABCFM Annual Reports (Eastern Turkey Mission); Barbara Reeves-Ellington, Domestic Frontiers (2013).
